source: Rhodes and Tauber (2011) The influence of delaying judgments of learning on metacognitive accuracy: a meta-analytic review (Psychological Bulletin 137(1):131-148)
finding: Two meta-analyses. Delaying the JOL gives a large gain in relative accuracy (gamma). The same delay gives only a tiny gain in actual memory.
numbers: Relative accuracy: g = 0.93, 4,554 participants, 112 effect sizes. Memory performance: g = 0.08, 3,807 participants, 98 effect sizes.
limits: Abstract read via PubMed; full text paywalled. The .70 and .03 values quoted by Tekin and Roediger are NOT in the abstract; probably subgroup or moderator values. g=.08 is the memory effect, not the accuracy effect.
agent_relevance: A delayed (post-attempt) judgment is far more diagnostic than an immediate one, but it does not make the answer itself better. Judge-after-draft is a monitor, not a booster.

source: Leonesio and Nelson (1990) Do different metamemory judgments tap the same underlying aspects of memory? (JEP:LMC 16(3):464-467)
finding: Ease-of-learning judgments made before study were the least accurate predictor of later memory among the judgment types tested. They correlated only weakly with judgments of knowing.
numbers: Undergraduates; EOL, then learning, then judgment of knowing, then 4 weeks later FOK and recognition. No gamma values in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC record). Word-list material.
agent_relevance: A pure from-the-prompt ease rating (our S0) is the weakest human monitor. Do not trust it alone; combine with a draft or a consistency cue.

source: Nelson et al. (1986) A comparison of three predictors of an individual's memory performance: own feeling of knowing, normative feeling of knowing, base-rate item difficulty (JEP:LMC 12(2):279-287)
finding: A person's own FOK predicted recognition better than normative FOK ratings, but worse than plain base-rate item difficulty (how often others got the item right).
numbers: General-information questions; recall failures rated for FOK; several criterion tests. No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Author list not shown in the record; check before citing authors.
agent_relevance: Strong point for S0: a table of past failure rates per task class can beat the model's own feeling. Log pass rates per class and use them as the gate.

source: Nelson and Leonesio (1988) Allocation of self-paced study time and the labor-in-vain effect (JEP:LMC 14(4):676-686)
finding: Ease-of-learning and FOK judgments are reliably linked to study time: more time goes to harder items. But large extra time sometimes gave little or no recall gain.
numbers: Three experiments, undergraduates, accuracy vs speed instructions. No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Authors not shown in the record.
agent_relevance: A gate that sends hard items to more compute is human-like, and can waste tokens on items where extra compute does not help. Cap the extra budget.

source: Koriat and Bjork (2005) Illusions of competence in monitoring one's knowledge during study (JEP:LMC 31(2):187-194)
finding: When the answer is visible at study, learners think they know it, but at test it is gone. Pairs with a strong after-the-fact link but a weak cue-alone link are overrated. Study-time JOLs track the pair link; later recall tracks the cue-alone link.
numbers: Paired-associates experiments. The abstract gives no effect sizes; I did not obtain them.
limits: Abstract only. Effect size for the illusion is NOT closed.
agent_relevance: Rating a problem while its solution or a worked solution is in view inflates confidence. Rate before seeing the answer or any solution hint.

source: Koriat (1993) How do we know that we know? The accessibility model of the feeling of knowing (Psychological Review 100(4):609-639)
finding: FOK comes from the same retrieval attempt used to find the target. It reflects how accessible related information is, right or wrong. Three experiments support this and argue against a privileged direct monitor.
numbers: Three experiments; no numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: A feeling of knowing is a by-product of a real retrieval attempt. A rating given without any attempt has less to draw on than one given after a short try.

source: Schwartz and Metcalfe (1992) Cue familiarity but not target retrievability enhances feeling-of-knowing judgments (JEP:LMC)
finding: Priming the question cues raised FOK. A manipulation that raised actual recall did not. Supports cue familiarity over target retrievability. Results mixed in experiments 3 and 4 (target priming helped only in 3).
numbers: Four experiments; participant numbers not in the record.
limits: Abstract only. Author names are my attribution; the record did not list them. Reder and Ritter (1992) was not retrieved.
agent_relevance: Familiar wording makes a prompt feel easy, whether or not the model can solve it. A gate based on wording is open to this bias.

source: Kornell, Rhodes, Castel and Tauber (2011) The ease-of-processing heuristic and the stability bias (Psychological Science 22(6):787-794)
finding: Type size changed predictions but not recall. Extra study changed recall but barely changed predictions. People also underestimated future learning (stability bias).
numbers: Three experiments; no effect sizes in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Authors not shown in the record.
agent_relevance: Fluent surface features inflate self-ratings in humans. Whether a clean or polished prompt inflates model self-ratings was not tested here.

source: Dunlosky and Nelson (1992) Importance of the kind of cue for judgments of learning and the delayed-JOL effect (Memory and Cognition 20(4):374-380)
finding: The delayed-JOL effect was very robust when the judgment cue was the stimulus alone (all 45 subjects showed it). It was small or absent when the cue was the whole stimulus-response pair.
numbers: 45 subjects; paired associates.
limits: Abstract only. Author names not shown in the record.
agent_relevance: The draft attempt must be made without the answer in view. A critique that sees the draft answer is a pair-cue judgment and may lose the advantage.

source: Episodic and semantic feeling-of-knowing in aging: a systematic review and meta-analysis (2023, Scientific Reports, PMC10542372)
finding: Older adults have worse episodic FOK accuracy than younger adults, but no age difference in semantic FOK. Funnel plot shows publication bias for episodic FOK.
numbers: 20 studies, 22 effects, 922 younger and 966 older adults. Episodic g = 0.53 [0.28, 0.78]; semantic g = -0.10 [-0.29, 0.10]; episodic Q(21)=102.77, total I2 79.09%; funnel asymmetry z=2.99, p=.003.
limits: Reports age differences only. It gives NO pooled absolute FOK accuracy for young adults. Hart (1965) and Nelson and Narens (1980) are not discussed. Last 5,694 characters unread.
agent_relevance: Semantic FOK (general knowledge) is stable and not age-sensitive, like LLM factual recall. Gap 3 (absolute FOK gamma) stays open.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Six reasoning models were better calibrated than their non-reasoning counterparts in 33 of 36 settings. The gain comes from slow-thinking behaviours (trying alternatives, backtracking). Calibration improves as the chain of thought unfolds; for non-reasoning models it gets worse.
numbers: Verbalised confidence, greedy decoding. TriviaQA AUROC about .65-.81 across models (table rows garbled in text extraction; EXAONE-3.5-Instruct about .65 at the low end, reasoning models about .75-.81). Example: GLM-Z1 vs GLM-4 on NonambigQA had 0.07 lower accuracy, yet 0.037 lower ECE and 0.078 higher AUROC. Non-reasoning Qwen2.5-Instruct put 85-95% confidence on more than 80% of samples. Counterexamples: GLM-4 on both SuperGPQA Math subsets and EXAONE-3.5-Instruct on the Non-Math subset had higher AUROC than their reasoning versions (multiple-choice cue artefact). Qwen3 thinking vs non-thinking (same checkpoint) differs in calibration.
limits: Open-weight 32B-class models, not frontier closed models. Confidence rarely drops below 55%. Table values partly garbled by PDF extraction; check before quoting single cells.
agent_relevance: Confidence after thinking is better than before thinking, so a post-draft rating beats a pre-draft rating. Supports reading confidence at the end of the draft, not at S0.

source: Mei et al. (2025) Reasoning about Uncertainty: Do Reasoning Models Know When They Don't Know? (arXiv 2506.18183)
finding: Reasoning models are typically overconfident, with verbalised confidence often above 85%, especially on wrong answers. Deeper reasoning makes them more overconfident. Self-introspection on the chain of thought helped o3-Mini and DeepSeek R1 but not consistently, and made Claude 3.7 Sonnet worse.
numbers: Abstract: confidence often above 85% on incorrect responses. No AUROC in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. This conflicts with Yoon et al. on whether more thinking helps; models, datasets and the way depth is varied differ.
agent_relevance: Do not assume longer thinking gives a better gate. Measure it on our own runs. Gap 6 is closed only as contested.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know (arXiv 2406.08391)
finding: About 1,000 graded examples with LoRA plus prompt give good uncertainty estimates and survive moderate distribution shift. A probe alone is worse than LoRA. A second model can be as good an estimator: Mistral-7B features applied to LLaMA-2 7B gave better AUROC than LLaMA-2 applied to itself.
numbers: Coding shift test (LiveCodeBench, Table 3), ECE / AUROC: LLaMA-2-7B zero-shot classifier 41.0 / 56.9, LoRA+Prompt 46.4 / 80.0; Mistral-7B zero-shot 70.2 / 66.2, LoRA+Prompt 21.4 / 85.1; Mistral-7B-Instruct zero-shot 52.7 / 47.1, LoRA+Prompt 56.1 / 70.2. KL regularisation: ECE 29.9 to 10.8, AUROC 70.2 to 71.6. As few as 1000 graded examples; 1000 points almost as valuable as 20,000.
limits: First 100,000 of 132,247 characters read. Several comparisons are in figures only. Calibration got slightly worse for two of three models under shift. Shift tested is mostly MMLU-style and code, not our agent's tasks.
agent_relevance: A trained gate on ~1,000 of our graded runs is plausible and can use a second model. But ECE can worsen under shift, so recalibrate when the task class changes (gaps 8 and 9).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification (arXiv 2504.05419)
finding: A probe on hidden states predicts correctness of intermediate answers, partly transfers across datasets, and works as an early-exit verifier that cuts tokens by about 24% with almost no accuracy loss.
numbers: Six reasoning models (R1-Distill 1.5B-70B, QwQ-32B); training sets capped at 1,000 examples. ROC-AUC above .7 in-distribution; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B above .9 on AIME. Transfer, R1-Distill-Llama-8B AUC / ECE: train GSM8K test MATH .80/.08, test AIME .69/.25, test KnowLogic .56/.10; train MATH test AIME .76/.28; train KnowLogic test GSM8K .77/.17, MATH .74/.19. MATH early exit: no exit 88.6%; threshold .85 gives 88.2% with about 24% fewer tokens; threshold .9 gives 88.6% with 19% fewer; static exit at the same tokens about 82.5%.
limits: AIME test sets are 25-30 items. Labels from Gemini 2.0 Flash. Training capped at 1,000. Logic-to-math transfer is poor. ECE degrades sharply on AIME.
agent_relevance: Math-to-math probe transfer is decent on ranking (AUC) but not on calibration. A gate trained on one task class needs a threshold reset for a new class.

source: Orgad et al. (2025) LLMs Know More Than They Show: On the Intrinsic Representation of LLM Hallucinations (arXiv 2410.02707)
finding: Error-detection probes work best at the exact-answer token. They do not generalise across tasks with different skills; there they are no better than logit baselines.
numbers: Probe AUC at exact answer token, TriviaQA / Winobias / Math: Mistral-7B-Instruct .85 / .92 / .92; Llama-3-8B-Instruct .83 / .93 / .95. End-of-question token: Mistral .76 / .82 / .72; Llama .77 / .80 / .72. Logit-min baseline: Mistral .75 / .53 / .71; Llama .79 / .61 / .89.
limits: First 100,000 of 161,341 characters read. Cross-task heatmap numbers not in the text; the no-better-than-logits claim is the authors' wording.
agent_relevance: A probe read before the answer (end of question) is clearly weaker (.72-.80) than one read at the answer token. Supports draft-then-judge over a pure pre-attempt gate. Transfers only within related skill families.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know - P(IK) sections 5.2 and 5.5, Tables 1 and 3
finding: P(IK) trained only on TriviaQA gives non-trivial AUROC on other tasks, but training on all tasks helps a lot, and calibration is poor on new distributions. Models are somewhat better at predicting their own P(IK) than another model's.
numbers: 52B classifiers. Table 1 AUROC / Brier (column labels garbled by extraction): TriviaQA-only values range .606 to .928; all-tasks-except-GSM8K values .752 to .987. Table 3 cross-experiment AUROC: A-init on A data .8633, on B data .8460; B-init on A data .8631, on B data .8717.
limits: Anthropic models only, 2022. GSM8K was the hardest case. Table cell labels uncertain from PDF extraction. Self-advantage is small (no difference on A data).
agent_relevance: A pre-answer gate learned on one class is only partly portable. Self-advantage is weak here, in contrast to Binder.

source: Binder et al. (2024) Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection (arXiv 2410.13787)
finding: Self-prediction of behaviour fails on tasks with long outputs, complex reasoning, or out-of-distribution properties. Self-advantage over a second model is real but modest and not found for every property.
numbers: Llama 70B self 48.5% vs GPT-4o predicting Llama 31.8% (the +17% headline is 16.7 points); GPT-4o self 49.4% vs Llama predicting GPT-4o 36.6%; cross-prediction plateau 35.2% beyond 10,000 samples; GPT-3.5 self-advantage +0.8%; sycophancy: Llama self 74.5% vs GPT-4o cross 76.5% (no advantage). 30,000 finetuning samples; 6 train and 6 held-out datasets.
quote: models failed to outperform baselines if the situation involves a longer response
limits: First 100,000 of 150,980 characters read. Trained self-prediction, not a prompt-only gate. Mainly short-answer properties.
agent_relevance: LLM analogue of Maki (1998): self-knowledge fails on long outputs. A gate for long multi-step tasks should not rely on self-prediction (gap 10, indirect support).

source: Lugoloobi and Russell (2025) LLMs Encode How Difficult Problems Are (arXiv 2510.18147)
finding: Human-labelled difficulty is linearly decodable from hidden states, and the signal grows with model size. Difficulty derived from the model's own failures is much weaker and gets worse during RL training.
numbers: Linear probes on 60 models; Easy2HardBench math and code. AMC human-difficulty rho about .88. During GRPO on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, the human-difficulty probe strengthened and correlated positively with test accuracy; the LLM-difficulty probe degraded and correlated negatively.
limits: Abstract only. Probe on hidden states, not a prompted easy/hard rating. The abstract does not say whether length or other surface cues were controlled.
agent_relevance: An ease-of-learning style signal exists inside the model before it answers (human-labelled difficulty). A prompted rating may not expose it. Gap 4 partly closed; the surface-cue control is still missing.

source: Shrivastava, Kumar and Liang (2025) Language Models Prefer What They Know: Relative Confidence Estimation via Confidence Preferences (arXiv 2502.01126)
finding: Asking a model which of two questions it is more likely to answer correctly, then aggregating (Elo or Bradley-Terry), beats asking for absolute confidence.
numbers: Five models (GPT-4, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1 405B), 14 tasks. Selective-classification AUC up 3.5% on average over absolute confidence and 1.7% over self-consistency.
limits: Abstract only. Needs many pairwise calls, so cost is higher than one rating; an equal-token comparison is not in the abstract.
agent_relevance: A comparative ease judgment (is A easier than B) is a better gate than a single score, but costs calls. Could be run against a bank of past tasks with known outcomes.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AdaptThink: Reasoning Models Can Learn When to Think (arXiv 2505.13417)
finding: A trained pre-answer policy chooses between thinking and no-thinking by difficulty. NoThinking is better and faster on easy problems.
numbers: Three math datasets; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: average response length down 53% and accuracy up 2.4%.
limits: Abstract only. RL-trained gate on a 1.5B model, math only. Not compared with a draft-then-judge scheme at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Best evidence that a pre-attempt difficulty gate saves compute without hurting accuracy. Gap 1 stays open: no head-to-head against a short draft.
